<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values across most models, indicating that a standard progress curve without initial product and with moderate catalyst/substrate concentrations is insufficient to strongly distinguish the mechanisms. 
- Models with product inhibition/deactivation (M5, M12, M17), catalyst dimerization/deactivation (M2, M3, M13, M18, M19), and substrate inhibition (M7, M11, M16) all fit the baseline data reasonably well. 
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but now we must perturb the system significantly to break this degeneracy and separate the models.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
By introducing a high initial product concentration (0.5), we can immediately activate product-dependent mechanisms (M5, M12, M17) from the very beginning of the reaction. This will distinctly alter the initial rate and the overall shape of the curve compared to models without product effects. Simultaneously, increasing the catalyst concentration to 0.2 (double the previous run) will amplify second-order catalyst interactions, such as dimerization (M2, M3) or bimolecular deactivation (M13, M18, M19). Lowering the substrate concentration to 1.0 will change the ratio of free catalyst to substrate-bound catalyst, further differentiating mechanisms that depend specifically on free `cat` (M9, M13) versus `catS` (M14, M18). This combination of changes will simultaneously probe product, catalyst, and substrate dependencies, effectively separating the currently clustered models.
</hypothesis>
